questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Who usually offers a 403(b) plan instead of a 401(k)?

choices.text: Every private technology company and its contractors
State and federal tax agencies to taxpayers
Banks to their savings customers
Public schools and many nonprofit organizations

questions.correct_answer: Public schools and many nonprofit organizations
questions.intro: A 401(k) is a retirement plan offered by many private employers. A 403(b) is a similar plan offered by public schools, colleges, hospitals, and many nonprofits. Both let workers save part of each paycheck, often with tax benefits and sometimes an employer match.
questions.feedback: 403(b) plans are common at public schools and nonprofits.

misconceptions.B: Confuses retirement plans with tax programs
misconceptions.C: Confuses an employer plan with a bank IRA

sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Raj earns $55,000. His employer matches 50% of his contributions up to 6% of pay. Raj contributes 6%. How much does the employer add per year?
questions.intro: An employer match adds money when you contribute. Contributing at least enough to get the full match is often called "free money."
questions.feedback: Raj contributes $55,000 × 0.06 = $3,300; the employer adds 50% = $1,650.
sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Raj contributes $3,300 to a traditional (pre-tax) 401(k), and his top federal tax rate is 12%. About how much federal income tax does this save this year?
questions.intro: Traditional 401(k) contributions are pre-tax: they lower taxable income now. Taxes are paid later on withdrawals. Roth 401(k) contributions are after-tax, with tax-free qualified withdrawals.
questions.feedback: $3,300 × 0.12 = $396 less federal tax this year.

misconceptions.D: Treats the contribution as tax saved
misconceptions.C: Gives the contribution minus the tax

sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Maya leaves a job with $10,000 in her 401(k) and is under 59½. If she cashes it out, assume 22% federal income tax plus a 10% additional tax for early withdrawal. How much is left?
questions.intro: When leaving a job, you can usually leave the money in the old plan, roll it into a new employer's plan, or roll it into an IRA. Cashing out before 59½ usually means income tax plus a 10% additional tax, unless an exception applies.
sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which choice usually keeps Maya's retirement money growing with taxes still deferred?

choices.text: A direct rollover to an IRA or new plan
Cashing out and spending it
Withdrawing it to pay for a vacation
Having a check mailed and keeping it for a year

questions.correct_answer: A direct rollover to an IRA or new plan
questions.intro: In a direct rollover, the old plan sends the money straight to the new IRA or plan, so taxes stay deferred.
questions.feedback: A direct rollover moves the money without taxes or penalties.
sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

sections.relationship: Match math depends on understanding that the employer adds money only when the worker contributes.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: What does an employer "match" mean?

choices.text: The employer pays the worker's taxes
The worker must repay the employer later, with interest added
The employer adds money based on what the worker contributes
The employer chooses the worker's investments

questions.correct_answer: The employer adds money based on what the worker contributes
questions.intro: With a match, the employer contributes to your retirement account in proportion to what you contribute, up to a limit.
questions.feedback: Matches reward your own contributions.
sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: A plan matches 100% up to 4% of pay. A worker earning $40,000 contributes 4%. How much is the match?
questions.intro: Match = matching rate × the worker's contribution, up to the plan's limit.
sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: If that worker contributes 0%, what is the match?
questions.intro: A match is paid only on what the worker contributes.
questions.feedback: No contribution means no match.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: What is "free money" in a 401(k)?

choices.text: Money that the government gives every worker each year
The employer match a worker receives by contributing
A loan from the plan
The tax refund a worker gets for contributing

questions.correct_answer: The employer match a worker receives by contributing
questions.feedback: The match is extra pay for saving.

misconceptions.A: Confuses the match with a government benefit
misconceptions.D: Confuses a match with a tax effect

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which statement about rolling a 401(k) into an IRA is TRUE?

choices.text: Every rollover is fully taxed
Rollovers are allowed only at age 65
A direct rollover avoids taxes and penalties
A check paid to her has no tax withheld

questions.correct_answer: A direct rollover avoids taxes and penalties
questions.intro: When you leave a job, you can roll a 401(k) into an IRA or a new employer plan. A direct (trustee-to-trustee) rollover avoids taxes and penalties.
questions.feedback: Direct rollovers keep tax deferral intact.

misconceptions.A: Confuses a rollover with a cash-out
misconceptions.D: Misses mandatory withholding on indirect rollovers

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: With an indirect rollover, the plan withholds 20% and the worker has 60 days to deposit the full amount into an IRA. On $10,000, how much is withheld?
questions.intro: If a plan pays the money to you instead of directly to the new account, it generally must withhold 20% for taxes; to avoid tax on the withheld part, you must make it up from other funds within 60 days.
sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

questions.prompt: In that indirect rollover, how much must the worker deposit within 60 days to avoid tax on any of the $10,000?

choices.text: $8,000 only
$2,000 only
Nothing; the rollover is fully automatic for him
$10,000, including $2,000 from other money

questions.intro: To complete the rollover tax-free, the full original amount must be deposited within 60 days.
questions.feedback: The full $10,000 must be redeposited; the withheld $2,000 comes back at tax time.

questions.prompt: Why might keeping a small old 401(k) in a former employer's plan be inconvenient?

choices.text: It is illegal to keep money in an old employer's plan
It is easy to lose track of old accounts
It stops earning returns once she leaves
The employer can take back her own contributions

questions.correct_answer: It is easy to lose track of old accounts
questions.intro: Old accounts left at many past employers can be forgotten. Consolidating can simplify tracking.
questions.feedback: Tracking many old accounts is hard; consolidation helps.

misconceptions.D: Confuses unvested match with her own money

Forget the account
Ask the employer to return all the money as cash

sections.skill: Plan features: auto-enrollment, Roth options, and loans

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Many plans auto-enroll new workers at 3% of pay unless they opt out. Why does auto-enrollment raise saving?

choices.text: People tend to keep the default
It doubles the match automatically
It removes all investment risk
It lowers the worker's salary

questions.correct_answer: People tend to keep the default
questions.intro: Defaults are powerful: when saving is automatic, most people keep it. Workers can usually change the rate or opt out.
questions.feedback: Default effects keep most auto-enrolled workers saving.
sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: A plan offers a Roth 401(k). How are contributions taxed?

choices.text: Never taxed at any time
Deducted now and taxed at withdrawal
Taxed now; qualified withdrawals later are tax-free
Taxed only if the market rises

questions.correct_answer: Taxed now; qualified withdrawals later are tax-free
questions.intro: Roth 401(k) contributions are after-tax. Qualified withdrawals, including earnings, are tax-free.
questions.feedback: Roth: pay tax now, tax-free qualified withdrawals later.

misconceptions.A: Confuses Roth with tax-free on both ends

sources: IRS (401(k) resource guide): 401(k) plans allow pre-tax or Roth employee deferrals and employer contributions; 403(b) plans are similar plans for public schools and certain nonprofits. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Some plans allow loans. Leo borrows $5,000 from his 401(k). What is a key risk?

choices.text: If he leaves his job, the loan may soon be due
Loans are always forgiven
The loan raises his credit score
There is no effect at all on his retirement savings

questions.correct_answer: If he leaves his job, the loan may soon be due
questions.intro: A 401(k) loan is repaid to your own account, but the money is not invested while borrowed, and leaving your job can make the remaining balance due quickly or treated as a taxable distribution.
questions.feedback: Job changes can turn an unpaid loan into a taxable distribution.

misconceptions.B: Believes 401(k) loans need not be repaid

A target-date fund
